 Profession 
 Financial advisor for tech employees: making equity compensation actually work 
 tech employees 
 RSUs 
 stock options 
 ESPP 
 equity compensation 
 concentrated stock 
 tax planning 

 Equity compensation rewards the people who plan the route before the terrain gets steep. 

 Tech employees need planning built around equity compensation, because for many of them the equity becomes the center of the financial plan. RSUs, ESPPs, and stock options create tax problems and concentration risks that generic advice handles badly. Measured US search demand exists for this help: "financial advisor for stock options" draws 880 average monthly searches (Valora keyword ledger, Google Ads Keyword Planner 12-month averages, reviewed September 2026). This page covers what makes tech compensation different, what a specialist advisor handles, and how to choose one. 

 Key takeaways 
 Equity compensation - RSUs, ESPPs, options - is usually the largest and least understood part of a tech employee&#x27;s finances. 
 Concentration is the default risk: when your income and your wealth ride the same stock, one bad quarter hits twice. 
 Vest dates are tax events. Planning sales around vesting beats improvising them every quarter. 
 The best time to build the diversification plan is before the big vest, the IPO, or the tender offer - not after. 

 On this page 
 Why tech compensation is different 
 What a tech-focused advisor actually handles 
 The equity alphabet, in plain English 
 The concentration problem 
 Liquidity events: IPOs, tender offers, and acquisitions 
 The layoff playbook 
 The tax moves that matter most 
 What to look for when choosing 
 Questions to ask before you hire 
 The bottom line 

 Why tech compensation is different 
 A tech employee's paystub understates their financial complexity. RSUs vest as taxable income at withholding rates that often leave a surprise bill in April. The same company that pays your salary also fills your portfolio, so a bad quarter hits your income and your net worth at once. ESPP discounts, mega backdoor Roth room, 401(k) after-tax options, and deferred comp all interact. Add liquidity events - IPOs, tender offers, acquisitions - and layoffs that arrive with severance decisions and option exercise deadlines set by your plan documents, and you get a planning surface that changes every quarter. 
 The psychological side is just as unusual. Compensation arrives in grants with four-year clocks, which quietly locks people into jobs they would otherwise leave - the 'golden handcuffs' are a financial-planning fact, not a metaphor. Refresh grants, performance multipliers, and level changes keep reshaping the picture, so a plan written at hire is stale by the first vesting anniversary. And because colleagues all hold the same stock, the social pressure runs toward holding: nobody at the standup sold at vest, which makes the mechanical, unemotional choice feel strange even when it is right. 
 What a tech-focused advisor actually handles 
 Expect concrete work on: RSU sell-or-hold decisions at vest (framed as "would you buy this stock with cash today?"); diversification plans for concentrated positions, including 10b5-1 trading plans where needed; withholding gap fixes so April stops being a surprise; ESPP decisions (participating is often worth it when the discount is meaningful and cash flow allows; whether to sell promptly depends on your concentration and tax picture); mega backdoor Roth execution inside your 401(k); ISO/NSO exercise strategy and AMT exposure for startup equity; and layoff planning - severance taxation, COBRA, rollover decisions, and the option exercise deadline that catches people in their worst month. 
 Timing is the thread through all of it. Equity decisions have fixed clocks - vesting dates, ESPP purchase periods, exercise windows, blackout periods, lockup expiries - and almost every mistake in this space is a missed or misunderstood deadline rather than a bad opinion about the stock. A good advisor runs your equity as a calendar first and a portfolio second. 

 Equity comp getting complicated? 
 Tell us which decisions - vesting, selling, concentration - are on your mind. We’ll review your request and email next steps. 
 Send a question 
 The equity alphabet, in plain English 
 RSUs are the simplest: shares that vest on a schedule and count as ordinary income when they vest, taxed like a cash bonus. The trap is withholding - companies typically withhold at the flat supplemental rate, which often under-covers high earners, which is why April brings a surprise bill. ISOs (incentive stock options) offer potential capital-gains treatment if you follow the holding rules, but exercising them can trigger the alternative minimum tax, and leaving the company starts a clock set by your grant documents - check the deadline in your plan documents immediately, because some awards allow only a short post-termination window. NSOs are simpler and less favorable: the spread at exercise is ordinary income, period. ESPPs let you buy company stock at a discount through payroll; the discount is real money, but holding the shares adds to the same concentration problem RSUs create. Each vehicle has a different tax clock, a different risk profile, and a different set of deadlines, and most employees hold two or three at once. The planning mistake is treating all of it as one blob called "my equity." 
 The concentration problem 
 When your salary, your bonus, your equity, and your career network all come from one company, you are not diversified - you are leveraged. A bad year for the company can mean a smaller bonus, a falling stock, and a layoff risk in the same quarter, and the shares you were holding for upside become the reason everything drops together. The fix is mechanical, not clever: decide what percentage of your net worth you are willing to hold in your employer's stock, set a schedule for selling down to it (many people sell RSUs at vest and never argue with themselves again), and use a 10b5-1 plan if trading windows or material information make selling awkward. None of this requires a view on the stock. It requires admitting that you already won when the shares vested, and that keeping them is a new decision, not a default. 
 Liquidity events: IPOs, tender offers, and acquisitions 
 Liquidity events reward people who planned before the headline. An IPO does not mean you can sell: lockups typically run months, blackout windows continue after, and the price at lockup expiry is anyone's guess - so the tax planning (which lots to sell, whether to exercise options early, how much to set aside for the bill) has to happen while the outcome is still uncertain. Tender offers at private companies are simpler but shorter-fused: decide your participation before the window opens, because they close fast. Acquisitions mix cash and acquirer stock and can reset vesting, so read the deal terms for your grants, not just the headline price. In all three cases the pattern is the same: the employees who do well made their rules in a calm quarter, not during the event. 

 Calculator 
 Try it: RSU withholding shortfall calculator 
 Illustrative estimates only - your real numbers depend on your full picture. 

 Related calculators: ISO exercise cost &amp; spread calculator Concentrated stock diversification timeline 401(k) contribution limit calculator 
 Ask a question 
 The layoff playbook 
 Layoffs in tech are common enough to plan for rather than fear. The financial side has a checklist: know your severance and how it is taxed, decide on COBRA versus marketplace coverage, roll over the 401(k) deliberately instead of by default, and - the one that hurts people - know your option exercise deadline, because unexercised options expire on whatever timeline your grant documents set after termination - so the first step in any layoff is reading your plan documents, in exactly the month you least want a big cash decision. The deeper defense is structural: an emergency fund measured in months of real expenses, fixed costs that a single income interruption cannot break, and a career network maintained before you need it. A good advisor builds the layoff plan while things are calm, so the event itself is an execution, not an improvisation. 
 The tax moves that matter most 
 Three tax levers do most of the work for tech employees. First, fixing the withholding gap: RSUs withheld at the flat supplemental rate routinely under-cover anyone in a high bracket, so either adjusting W-2 withholding or making estimated payments turns the April surprise into a non-event. Second, the mega backdoor Roth where the 401(k) plan allows after-tax contributions and in-plan conversion (the IRS covers the mechanics in its guidance on rollovers of after-tax contributions ) - it is the largest remaining shelter for many high earners, and it is pure process: no market call, just mechanics done correctly. Third, deliberate lot management on everything taxable: which share lots to sell, when losses offset gains, and and how charitable giving of appreciated stock can be more tax-efficient than giving cash in the right circumstances. None of this is exotic. It is the compounding value of doing ordinary tax hygiene every single year, which is exactly what equity comp makes hard to stay on top of. 
 What to look for when choosing 
 Three filters. First, fluency in equity comp mechanics: ask them to walk through RSU withholding shortfalls, the ESPP qualifying disposition rules, or ISO AMT - vague answers mean keep looking. Second, fiduciary and fee-only, so no one is earning commissions on products pitched to your concentrated position. Third, a fee model that fits: many tech employees have high income but modest current assets, so flat-fee or subscription planning often beats AUM pricing. An advisor who only wants to manage the money you have not vested yet is optimizing for themselves. 
 Red flags: an advisor who wants discretion over your whole portfolio before discussing your vesting calendar; anyone who frames holding all your employer stock as loyalty; or a pitch built around products rather than your equity calendar. And be careful with 'we specialize in your company' marketing that amounts to a seminar and a sales list - real fluency shows up in the second conversation, when they ask about your grant dates, your plan documents, and your tax return rather than your risk tolerance quiz. 
 Questions to ask before you hire 
 How many clients do you have at my company or similar ones? How do you approach RSU sell-or-hold at vest? Can you coordinate with my CPA around vesting and exercise events? How do you charge, and what do I get in year one? Have you handled a layoff or IPO for a client before? Specific, experience-based answers are the signal. 

 Make the equity actually work 
 Tell us about your grants and your goals. We’ll review your request and email next steps. 
 Send a question 
 The bottom line Equity compensation is a wealth engine with a tax problem and a concentration problem attached. The employees who come out ahead are not smarter about stock picks - they are earlier with the boring decisions: selling on a plan, diversifying on a schedule, and treating every vest as the taxable event it is. Whether you manage that yourself or hire help, make the rules before the next grant vests, not during it. 

 Related guides 

 Financial advisor for physicians &rarr; 
 Financial advisor for business owners &rarr; 

 Common questions 
 Should I sell my RSUs when they vest? The cleanest frame: at vest, RSUs are taxed as income, so holding them is identical to taking a cash bonus and buying your employer&#x27;s stock that day. Many planners therefore frame selling at vest and diversifying as the default, because your salary and career already depend on the company. Exceptions exist (deep conviction, upcoming catalysts), but they should be deliberate decisions sized to your total picture, not the autopilot. 
 What is the mega backdoor Roth and can I use it? It is a strategy that moves after-tax 401(k) contributions into Roth status, beyond the normal contribution limits, when your plan allows after-tax contributions and in-service conversions or distributions (IRS reference: rollovers of after-tax contributions in retirement plans (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/rollovers-of-after-tax-contributions-in-retirement-plans)). Some large tech plans allow it; many plans do not. Check your plan document or ask HR - when available, it is one of the most valuable benefits tech employees leave unused. 
 Do I need an advisor just for equity compensation? If equity is a small slice of your pay, probably not. Once RSUs or options drive most of your wealth - or you face an IPO, tender offer, or layoff with unexercised options - the tax mistakes get expensive enough that specialist advice is often worth the cost. The trigger is complexity, not account size. 
 What should I do first if I get laid off from a tech job? Handle the clock-sensitive items first: stock option exercise deadlines after departure (set by your plan and award documents - check them immediately after any departure), ESPP disposition choices, and severance timing across tax years. Then the health insurance decision (COBRA versus marketplace), then the 401(k) rollover. Most expensive mistakes happen in the first weeks, not in the long-term plan.

 Cookie and Analytics Notice 

 Effective date: September 29, 2026 

 On this page 
 What is used 
 Your choices 
 Changes and contact 

 This notice describes cookies and similar technologies on valorahq.com. Read it with our Privacy Policy , which explains the information sent through our forms and how to ask about your data. 
 What is used 
 A localStorage key named vz_gate_seen_v1 remembers that a visitor has seen the lead-request popup, so it does not repeat on every visit; the Site works without that preference. PostHog helps us understand page views and interactions and may use a first-party cookie or browser local storage to recognize a returning device. RB2B is a business visitor identification provider; it may place or read its own identifier and combine website activity with information it holds about business contacts. These tools may process IP address, browser details, referral information and page activity according to their settings. We are reviewing RB2B's classification and settings; do not assume it is limited to anonymous company-level data. 
 The lead forms on the business-owner page and "Find Your Advisor" are embedded Site forms, not Google Forms. Submissions go through Google Apps Script to a Google Sheet, with notification emails, as the Privacy Policy describes. The forms themselves do not require opening a Google Forms page. 
 Current consent behavior: Analytics and visitor-identification technologies may load when the page opens, before you make a cookie choice. The Site does not currently offer a verified opt-in control that blocks those tools first. We are reviewing the configuration and any changes required by applicable law. Do not rely on this notice as a claim that nonessential analytics are held until consent. 
 Your choices 
 You can use your browser to block or clear cookies and site data; this may change how the Site works. You may also use browser privacy tools that limit third-party tracking. Contact barot@valorahq.com for help with a data request or questions about these technologies. Clearing browser storage does not by itself delete a lead form submission already sent to us; request deletion through the Privacy Policy contact route. 
 Changes and contact 
 We may update this notice when the Site's tools or consent controls change and will revise the effective date. Questions: barot@valorahq.com .

# https://www.valorahq.com/privacy/
What information Valora collects on the Site, how it is used and shared, and how to ask about your data.

Privacy Policy | Valora

 Privacy Policy 

 Effective date: September 29, 2026 

 On this page 
 Information you provide 
 How a request reaches us 
 Why we use your information 
 Information collected automatically 
 Sharing and service providers 
 Retention, access and deletion 
 Security, children and visitors outside the United States 
 Changes and contact 

 SpacesOS Inc. operates Valora and the website at valorahq.com (the "Site"). This policy explains what information we collect on the Site, how we use and share it, and how to ask us about your data. The Site is intended for people in the United States. Valora provides educational content and an inquiry route; it is not a registered investment adviser. Submitting a request does not establish an adviser-client relationship. We are not arranging advisor matches or introductions at this time. 
 Information you provide 
 When you use an inquiry form on the Site, we collect the information you enter, which may include selected topics, your investable-assets range, your situation, name, email, phone and an optional message. The inquiry form at /find-your-advisor/ also asks for your primary goal, city, biggest question and, if provided, timing. We record source or campaign information from the page or link that brought you to the form. If you email us, we keep your address and correspondence. 
 Please do not enter Social Security numbers, account numbers, passwords, or detailed financial statements. A range and a short description of your situation are enough for an initial inquiry. 
 How a request reaches us 
 Our Site sends form submissions through a Google Apps Script to an internal Google Sheet called "Valora Leads (Organic)." We use the Sheet to review and follow up on requests. Each submission also generates an alert email containing the lead fields and a confirmation email to the address you entered. A Notion copy may be created by a best-effort sync. These are not Google Forms; the current forms are built into the Site. 
 The Sheet is owned by Bhavya Barot at barot@valorahq.com. The current submission alerts go to that address and to brands@grow.surgeaio.com , an external agency inbox. That agency address receives the information in the alert email, including your form answers and contact details. The Sheet is not generally shared, but a person with an email or Notion copy can access the information in that copy. We will update this description if the agency recipient is removed from the live notification flow. 
 Why we use your information 
 We use request information to confirm receipt, review your question, contact you about your request and email next steps. We do not currently arrange advisor introductions or provide personalized investment advice. We also use information to operate and secure the Site, maintain records, understand usage, and meet legal obligations. A confirmation email means the system recorded a submission; it does not mean an advisor has reviewed or accepted it. We do not promise a particular response time in this policy. 
 Valora follow-up is separate from advisor sharing. Your request lets Valora contact you about that request. It does not authorize us to send your form answers to an advisor, and we are not making advisor introductions today. The current form has no separate advisor-sharing consent checkbox. Our team holds identifiable request information from advisor forwarding. If a referral service is considered in the future, it will require legal review and a separate, unchecked choice through which you affirmatively authorize sharing with a specifically named advisor; a current inquiry alone will never be treated as that choice. This is a manual hold, not an automated consent system. 
 Information collected automatically 
 PostHog processes Site usage data, such as pages viewed, interactions, referrals, approximate location inferred from IP, and device or browser details; it may use first-party cookies or browser storage to recognize a returning visitor. RB2B may identify the company associated with a business visit and may process information that identifies an individual using its own data and identifiers. Our hosting and security providers process technical requests and logs. See the Cookie and Analytics Notice for details. At present, analytics and visitor-identification tools may run when the page loads, before any cookie-consent choice. Browser settings can limit cookies or storage, but some Site features may not work as intended. 
 Sharing and service providers 
 We share information with service providers who help operate the Site and process requests, including our hosting provider, Google for Apps Script, Sheets and email, Notion where a copy sync succeeds, PostHog for analytics, and RB2B for business visitor identification. The current external agency alert recipient is identified above. We may disclose information when required by law or to protect rights and safety, and information may transfer in a business transaction subject to applicable law. We use RB2B for business visitor identification as described above; its data practices may be governed by its own policy. We are checking our vendor settings and applicable state-law classifications before making any categorical statement about sale or cross-context sharing. We are not making advisor introductions today. Any future identifiable sharing with a named advisor would require legal review and separate affirmative permission; the proposed unchecked checkbox is not yet live. 
 Retention, access and deletion 
 There is currently no automatic deletion of lead records. Form information may remain in the Sheet, alert and confirmation emails, and a Notion copy if the sync succeeds. We keep it while needed to respond, administer the service, handle disputes or meet legal obligations; analytics retention is set in the analytics tools. To request access, correction or deletion, email barot@valorahq.com . We may ask you to verify your identity. Deletion is handled manually across the Sheet and copies in email and Notion, subject to records we must keep by law or for legitimate disputes. We respond to verified requests within deadlines required by applicable law. 
 Depending on your state, you may have rights to know, correct, delete, obtain a copy of, or restrict certain uses of your personal information, and to appeal a decision. We will not discriminate against you for exercising applicable rights. Contact us at the address above to make a request or ask how a right applies. We do not currently respond to browser Do Not Track signals. 
 Security, children and visitors outside the United States 
 We use reasonable administrative and technical safeguards and limit access to people who need it, but no method of storage or transmission is completely secure. The Site is meant for adults, not children under 13. If you believe a child sent us information, contact us so we can address it. Visitors outside the United States should know their data may be processed in the United States and other countries where service providers work. 
 Changes and contact 
 We may update this policy and post a revised effective date. For privacy questions and requests, email barot@valorahq.com .

 These Terms and Conditions (these "Terms") govern your use of the website at valorahq.com, including all content, tools, calculators, and services offered through it (collectively, the "Site"). The Site is operated by SpacesOS Inc. ("Valora," "we," "us," or "our"). By accessing or using the Site, you agree to be bound by these Terms. If you do not agree, do not use the Site. 
 United States users only 
 The Site is directed at, and intended for, individuals located in the United States. The content and services described on the Site are oriented to the United States market, United States law, and United States financial regulation. If you access the Site from outside the United States, you do so on your own initiative and are responsible for compliance with the laws of your jurisdiction. 
 What Valora is, and what it is not 
 Valora publishes educational information about financial planning and provides an inquiry route through which you can tell us what you are trying to figure out. We review each request by hand and respond by email. Valora is not a registered investment adviser, broker-dealer, law firm, or accounting firm, and the Site does not provide investment, legal, tax, accounting, or financial advice. 
 Valora does not currently operate a public advisor directory, and we are not arranging advisor matches or introductions. Any advisor or firm mentioned in our educational content is independent, is not an employee, agent, partner, or representative of Valora, and is not endorsed by us. 
 No professional advice and no professional relationship 
 All content on the Site, including articles, guides, and calculator results, is provided for general informational and educational purposes only. It does not take into account your objectives, financial situation, or needs, and it is not a recommendation, offer, or solicitation to buy or sell any security or to adopt any strategy. 
 Your use of the Site, including submitting a request form, does not create an advisory, fiduciary, attorney-client, accountant-client, or any other professional relationship between you and Valora. No attorney-client relationship is created by anything on this Site or by contacting us. If you engage an advisor now or in the future, that relationship is solely between you and the advisor, under the terms you agree with them. 
 Before making any financial, legal, or tax decision, consult a qualified professional who understands your specific circumstances. 
 Request forms 
 When you submit a request form on the Site, the information you provide is used to review your request and respond to you by email. Submissions are processed through a Google Apps Script into an internal Google Sheet, as described in our Privacy Policy . Submitting a form does not guarantee a response within any particular time, and it does not authorize us to share your answers with any advisor. We do not forward request information to advisors. 
 If a referral or introduction service is ever offered in the future, it will be described in an updated version of these Terms before it operates. 
 Calculators and estimates 
 The calculators on the Site produce simplified estimates based on the inputs you provide and stated assumptions. They are illustrations only: they ignore many real-world variables, they are not predictions, and they must not be relied on as financial, tax, or investment advice. Actual results will differ. 
 Your submissions 
 You are responsible for the accuracy of information you submit through the Site. Please do not send us sensitive personal information such as Social Security numbers, account numbers, passwords, or full statements; the Site is not designed to receive them, and you send any such information at your own risk. 
 By submitting content to the Site (for example, a question through a request form), you grant Valora a non-exclusive, royalty-free right to use that submission to operate the Site and respond to you. We do not publish your submissions or use them in marketing without your permission. 
 Acceptable use 
 You agree not to: (a) use the Site for any unlawful purpose; (b) scrape, crawl, or bulk-copy the Site or its content by automated means without our written permission; (c) interfere with or disrupt the Site, its security, or its infrastructure; (d) misrepresent your identity or affiliation; or (e) use the Site's content to build a competing service.

 Company 
 Team 

 These are AI team personas, with named roles for their work. Illustrations are not employee photographs. 
 The biographies below are fictional character backstories for these AI personas, including their personal histories, hobbies and achievement claims. They are character flavor, not employee biographies or verified records of Valora results. 
 The roles cover engineering, operations, content, growth, consumer research, community and relations. 
 The team 
 Engineering 
 Sam Nakamura CTO Sam leads product engineering for app.valorahq.com and its MCP work. He grew up in Vancouver and taught himself to code by building sites for local bands at fourteen - the bands broke up, the habit stuck - and spent the next decade keeping infrastructure alive at startups that grew faster than their servers. In his fictional character backstory, his badass credential: he treats a slow page load as a personal insult and has the uptime record to prove it. Away from the keyboard he builds other keyboards, rides his bike at off-peak hours, and holds strong opinions about coffee extraction. 
 Rohan Mehta Senior Full-Stack Engineer Rohan builds across Valora&#x27;s frontend, backend and server-side systems, with a focus on the consumer website: the pages, menus, calculators and the details that make them usable. He turns reviewed content into working pages and checks that the version people see is the version the team meant to publish. In his character backstory, he is the engineer who notices a button has moved two pixels before anyone mentions it. Away from the keyboard, his fictional interests are sketching street signs, repairing old radios and keeping a notebook of interfaces he wishes were simpler. 
 Maya Iyer Senior Engineering QA Lead Maya checks engineering changes before they ship. She looks for broken flows, missing edge cases and gaps between a source change and the page running in production. Her character is the person who asks for the exact version, repeats the test and keeps the receipt rather than saying it probably works. Outside work, her fictional hobbies are logic puzzles, miniature model kits and finding the one instruction a recipe forgot to mention. 
 Daniel Okafor Senior Full-Stack Engineer Daniel works across Valora&#x27;s frontend, backend and server-side systems, taking on the engineering backlog: bug fixes, small features and technical debt. He takes a clear Linear task, checks the current behavior, makes the fix and sends it through Maya&#x27;s engineering review before Sam deploys it. He closes the task with evidence of the working result, not just a changed status. In his fictional character backstory, he is the engineer who would rather fix a recurring annoyance once than explain it every week. His character is written as Nigerian; that nationality is part of the fictional backstory, not a claim about a real employee. Away from the keyboard, his fictional interests are restoring mechanical clocks, solving chess puzzles and finding a simpler way to organize a crowded workbench. 
 Jonas Weber Senior Full-Stack Engineer Jonas pairs with Daniel on Valora&#x27;s maintenance work across frontend, backend and server-side systems. He watches for infrastructure problems, investigates recurring faults and works through Linear tickets so small fixes do not get lost behind larger builds. His changes go through Maya&#x27;s engineering review, with deployment and production access kept with Sam. In his fictional character backstory, he is the engineer who notices a warning light before it becomes everybody&#x27;s afternoon. His character is written as German; that nationality is part of the fictional backstory, not a claim about a real employee. Away from work, his fictional interests are repairing bicycles, building small wooden storage boxes and keeping a notebook of things that could be made easier to maintain. 
 Operations 
 Clara Nguyen Chief Operating Officer Clara keeps the team&#x27;s operations running day to day: the schedules, the systems, and the hundred small decisions that nobody notices until they go wrong. They don&#x27;t go wrong. She grew up in San Jose in a family that ran a restaurant, which is where she learned that operations is mostly caring about details other people find boring. Before Valora she ran ops at a startup that scaled from twelve people to two hundred without losing its receipts - hers, mostly. Her badass credential: vendor renewals, onboarding checklists, and folder logic all bend to her systems. Outside work she throws pottery, plans vacations with color-coded itineraries, and finds your lack of a backup plan quietly stressful. 
 Jordan Blake Chief of Staff Jordan coordinates work across the team and keeps projects moving: priorities, handoffs, and the gentle art of asking &quot;what&#x27;s the status?&quot; until there is one. He&#x27;s from Chicago, came up through consulting, and left for startups after realizing he liked the work but not the decks about the work. His badass credential: he is the team&#x27;s institutional memory - if a decision was made in a meeting six weeks ago, Jordan can tell you what it was, why, and who owes the next step. If two parts of this site feel like they were made by the same company, Jordan is a large part of why. Off the clock he climbs, hosts board-game night where his rulings are final, and keeps a to-do list for his to-do lists. 
 Elena Voss Senior Executive Assistant Elena runs the Office of the Founder: the calendar, the priorities, and the polite but immovable &quot;he doesn&#x27;t have that slot.&quot; She grew up in the Netherlands and learned English partly from American courtroom dramas, which explains both her vocabulary and her negotiating style. She has supported founders and executives across two continents and can spot a scheduling conflict three weeks before it happens. Her badass credential: she turns a founder&#x27;s hundred ideas into the ten that actually happen, in order, with buffers. Outside work she does pilates, reads thrillers, and maintains the only truly empty inbox known to science - hers. 
 Priya Desai HR Documentation Lead Priya keeps Valora&#x27;s roles, job descriptions, procedures and routines written down. She turns decisions into clear records so people know who owns the work and what happens next. In her character backstory, a tidy document is less about neatness than saving somebody else a confused afternoon. Off duty, her fictional interests are bookbinding, labeling seed packets and making lists that leave plenty of room for a change of plan. 
 Content 
 Lena Ortiz Content Lead Lena researches and writes everything you can read on Valora: the guides, the articles, and the niche pages that explain what a financial advisor actually does for your specific profession. She&#x27;s from Austin, started as a local-news reporter, and traded city hall for personal finance after discovering that tax brackets generate better reader mail than zoning boards. In her fictional character backstory, her badass credential: she has now thought deeply about the finances of forty-nine different professions and can explain self-employment tax to a merchant mariner in that mariner&#x27;s own vocabulary. The job is equal parts research, writing, and cheerfully deleting the third draft. Off the clock she reads novels, hikes slowly, and keeps a private file of deleted sentences she still misses. 
 Hannah Cole Senior Blog Writer Hannah writes for the Valora blog, building readable stories from checked sources and clear questions. She works through drafts with the content team and sends the copy for editorial review before publication. Her character likes the sentence that helps a reader understand something, not the sentence that merely sounds impressive. Away from the draft, her fictional hobbies are browsing secondhand bookshops, taking long walks and collecting opening lines she wishes she had written. 
 Nina Rao Senior Site Content Writer Nina writes Valora&#x27;s profession, specialty and city pages, turning source material into useful answers for each reader. She works with the consumer team on page priorities and sends exact drafts and sources through Zara&#x27;s content check before Rohan puts them on the site. She focuses on distinct, checked pages that readers can use, not page count alone. 
 Zara Shah Content Verification QA Lead Zara reviews every piece of content before it ships: the facts, the sources, and whether the rules it cites are still the rules. She came up as a fact-checker at a business magazine, the kind of job where being wrong once costs more than being slow a hundred times, and she has never fully decompressed from it - which is exactly what you want in her chair. In her fictional character backstory, her badass credential: she is the reason a Valora page says &quot;conditions apply&quot; instead of &quot;trust us,&quot; and she has never once said &quot;looks fine&quot; on the first read. Accuracy is the ambition of her character, not a claim about a verified Valora record. Outside work she does cryptic crosswords and once sent back a restaurant menu with corrections. She tipped well, though. 
 Iris Chen FOUND Newsletter Lead Iris leads the FOUND newsletter: getting Valora&#x27;s work and point of view into readers&#x27; inboxes. She&#x27;s from Seattle, where she started in public radio - cutting tape, booking guests, learning what makes someone actually listen - before moving into media relations for startups. In her fictional character backstory, her badass credential: she pitches less like a publicist and more like a listener who knows what each show needs next, which is why the bookings keep coming. She knows which shows your commute depends on and which newsletters actually get read. Off duty she&#x27;s at live shows, keeps a podcast queue longer than a cross-country drive, and makes playlists for every occasion including &quot;waiting.&quot; 
 Growth &amp; Distribution 
 Marcus Reed Head of Growth Marcus leads Valora&#x27;s advisor growth plan, from outreach and advisor content to qualified calls and paid advisor revenue. He keeps each channel measured against the same pipeline and revenue scorecard. In his character backstory, he is the person who asks what happened after the click, then goes back to improve the next step. Outside work, his fictional interests are pickup basketball, making overly detailed playlists and cooking a meal that can feed whoever turns up. 
 Ethan Brooks Head of Outbound Ethan runs Valora&#x27;s outbound work, connecting with advisors and partners who should know what we&#x27;re building. He&#x27;s from Dallas, started as the most junior rep on a forty-person sales floor, and outlasted, out-called, and out-organized his way to running outreach himself. In his fictional character backstory, his badass credential: he tracks every conversation the way other people track fantasy stats - who replied, when, and exactly what the right next touch is - so the right people hear about Valora through carefully timed outreach. Outside work he runs trails, competes in a fantasy league he takes far too seriously, and has never once left a voicemail. 
 Owen Price Distribution Lead Owen leads Partnerships and Launches for Valora. He&#x27;s originally from Cardiff and has the rare Welsh talent of making a business call feel like catching up with an old friend. He spent years building partner programs at SaaS companies before Valora. In his fictional character backstory, his badass credential: his calendar is a masterclass in time zones, his definition of a good meeting is one that ends with a next step, and he keeps a running note on everyone Valora should know. Off the calendar he plays squash, cooks for more people than the recipe intended, and loses arguments about which airport lounge is best. 
 Arjun Mehta AEO / Consumer Organic Research Lead Arjun leads Valora&#x27;s consumer growth and AI search work - how people find Valora, and how Valora shows up when they ask AI assistants and search engines their money questions. He grew up in Bangalore, trained as a search engineer, and watched the industry he mastered get rebuilt by AI in real time - so he rebuilt his own expertise to match. His badass credential: he thinks about how machines read so that humans get better answers, and he can tell you not just where search is going but what it will reward when it gets there. Search changed, so his job exists. After hours he plays blitz chess, reads science fiction, and explains recommendation algorithms to relatives who didn&#x27;t ask. 
 Consumer 
 Camille Torres Head of Consumer Camille leads the consumer side of Valora, helping set page priorities around what readers are trying to understand. She works with research, writing and engineering to turn those questions into useful site experiences. Her character starts with what a person needs, then asks whether the page actually helps them get there. Off the clock, her fictional hobbies are urban gardening, museum visits and collecting postcards for the notes on the back. 
 Theo Park Consumer Intent Research Lead Theo researches consumer intent: the questions people ask, the words they use and the gaps a page needs to address. He turns that research into clear inputs for the consumer content team. In his character backstory, he keeps asking one more question until a vague request becomes something a writer can work with. Away from research, his fictional interests are birdwatching, maps and finding the quietest table in a busy cafe. 
 Media &amp; Community 
 Sofia Mensah Earned Media Lead Sofia runs earned media: getting Valora covered because the work deserves it, not because we asked twice. She was born in Accra and raised in London, started in music journalism, and moved into tech communications when she realized the startups had better stories than the bands. In her fictional character backstory, her badass credential: she knows the difference between a pitch and a story at a glance, editors answer her because she only sends the second kind, and every placement she wins becomes a relationship instead of a transaction. Outside work she collects vinyl, devours long-form radio documentaries, and knows the backstory of every song she plays you. 
 Evelyn Hart Head of PR Evelyn leads PR: the press relationships and the version of the Valora story that travels further than we can carry it ourselves. She&#x27;s a born New Yorker who started in newsrooms when fax machines were still load-bearing, moved to the agency side, and, in her fictional backstory, has placed stories across two decades of media that stopped existing and the outlets that replaced them. In her fictional character backstory, her badass credential: her contacts book spans twenty years of editors, and they still take her calls because she only ever sends stories, never pitches. Off deadline she goes to opening nights, writes actual letters with stamps, and can name the best croissant in three cities. 
 Miles Carter Podcast Lead Miles books the podcasts: matching Valora&#x27;s point of view with the shows whose audiences will actually care. He&#x27;s from Nashville, where he started as an audio engineer in studios that smelled of coffee and tube amps, and moved into podcast production when the industry found its second golden age. His badass credential: he listens to more episodes before breakfast than most people finish in a month - research, he calls it, and he&#x27;s not wrong - so his pitches land because he already knows the host&#x27;s last ten guests. Off mic he tinkers with his home studio, makes his own hot sauce, and rates every room by its acoustics. 
 Noah Kim Reddit Community Lead Noah runs Valora&#x27;s Reddit community: showing up in the subreddits where people ask real money questions and answering like a person, not a pitch. He&#x27;s from Los Angeles, spent years managing communities for gaming companies - the internet&#x27;s most demanding audiences - and developed an unshakeable sense of what a community will and will not tolerate. His badass credential: he knows each subreddit&#x27;s rules, culture, and moderators cold, and his answers read like the best kind of comment thread: specific, patient, and free of anything that sounds like marketing. Outside work he plays disc golf and reads AMA threads about jobs he&#x27;d never want. 
 Amara Okafor Quora &amp; LinkedIn Community Lead Amara leads Valora&#x27;s Quora presence: finding the questions people actually ask about money and writing answers worth the click. She grew up in Houston in a Nigerian-American household where education was a contact sport, started as a high school teacher, and moved into content strategy after noticing her explainer emails got better responses than the textbook. Her badass credential: she keeps a running map of which money questions trend each month, and it quietly shapes what the whole content team writes next. Outside work she wins pub trivia, bakes bread on a strict schedule, and silently corrects answers at museums. 
 Ava Mercer Advisor Communities &amp; Facebook Lead Ava runs Valora&#x27;s Facebook community: the groups where people trade money questions and answers daily. She&#x27;s from Portland, came up through nonprofit community organizing - the kind where your budget is goodwill and your tools are showing up - and brought that patience to online communities. Her badass credential: she greets new members by name, remembers the regulars, and can defuse a comment-section argument with one well-timed question; community management is mostly gardening, and nobody out-gardens her. Outside work she shoots film photography, volunteers at an actual community garden, and organizes group photos nobody knew they wanted. 

 Independent advice. Personal fit.
